references.text: The Lord warns Moses that the people must not break through to see the Lord, or many of them will die. This underscores the same theme that humans cannot see God and live.
Jacob expresses surprise that he has seen God face to face and yet survived, confirming the belief that seeing God would normally lead to death.
Gideon fears he will die because he has seen the angel of the Lord face to face. The Lord assures him that he will not die.
Manoah tells his wife they will die because they have seen God, reflecting the same belief that seeing God means death.
Isaiah cries woe to himself because he has seen the Lord, the God of hosts, with his own eyes. This shows the fear of seeing God.
John writes that no one has ever seen God, but the only Son has made him known. This confirms that God is invisible to humans.
Jesus says that no one has seen the Father except the one who is from God. This emphasizes God's invisibility to humans.
Paul describes God as the one who dwells in unapproachable light, whom no human has seen or can see. This confirms that humans cannot see God.
John writes that no one has ever seen God, but if we love one another, God lives in us. This repeats the theme of God's invisibility.
Isaiah's near-death confirmation that he cannot see the Lord in the land of the living concretely and personally illustrates the absolute principle God established for Moses.
A clear contrast between a human threat (Pharaoh) and a divine reality (God), where both use 'see my face' to describe death, but with different sources and theological weight.
